newsitem.title: THAILAND: Offshore baht/dlr surges over onshore rates.
newsitem.headline: Offshore baht/dlr surges over onshore rates.

text.p: The baht rallied strongly against the dollar in the offshore currency market on Friday as the currency's surging foreign rate sharply widened its gap with that quoted in the domestic market, dealers said.

Dealers said the baht firmed to an intraday high of 24.840 to the dollar in offshore markets before it retreated to about 25.120/25.220 at 0748 GMT. The rate compared with a domestic low of 25.830 quoted by Thai-based dealers.

A two-tier offshore and onshore baht market has been in place since mid-May, after speculative attacks on the currency, when the central bank imposed capital controls to cut off baht supplies at local rates to offshore players.

Dealers said the stronger offshore baht reflected higher foreign demand for the currency, most likely from speculators, seeking to cover their short-baht positions taken earlier after their failed attacks on the currency. Dealers said the stronger offshore baht reflected higher foreign demand for the currency, most likely from speculators, seeking to cover their short-baht positions taken earlier after their failed attacks on the currency. The Bank of Thailand in coordination with other regional central banks intervened heavily in the market during the mid-May speculative attacks to fend off speculators. The Bank of Thailand also ordered local banks to quote higher baht rates to foreign players.

"The desperate foreign bids for the baht today showed that some of those baht/dollar speculative deals matured and parties involved need to cover themselves by choosing to sell dollars for the firmer baht rather than to roll over their positions by paying even more costly forward premiums," a dealer at a foreign bank said.
The one-month forward premium was quoted at about 100/140 satangs per dollar in offshore markets against 20/35 satangs quoted for domestic transactions.
Prior to the two-tier exchange rate system introduced this month, the one-month premium hovered at only six to eight satangs.
"We heard one foreign forward deal for five (million) dollars done at 105 (satang premium) this morning," a dealer said, adding that trade in offshore baht was very thin on Friday.
Dealers said, however, that the stronger offshore baht did not necessarily reflect improved sentiment in the Thai currency, its financial institutions or the economy.

The dealers said they had seen no clear signs that the Thai capital control had hampered trade-related foreign exchange transactions although it was not clear how long the government could impose the two-tier system without disrupting trade and normal capital flows.
The central bank has said it will review the two-tier market from time to time, while analysts have warned it could hurt Thailand's long term image as a liberal financial centre.
